4332.answer: All evidence should be taken in the presence of the accused, or, when his personal attendance is dispensed with, in the presence of his pleader.

4333.question: Who should be present when evidence is being taken during a trial or other proceeding?
4333.answer: All evidence should be taken in the presence of the accused, or, when his personal attendance is dispensed with, in the presence of his pleader.

4334.question: What provision is made in the text regarding the evidence of a woman below the age of eighteen years who is alleged to have been subjected to rape or any other sexual offence?
4334.answer: The court may take appropriate measures to ensure that such woman is not confronted by the accused while at the same time ensuring the right of cross-examination of the accused.

4335.question: What measures may the court take when a woman below the age of eighteen years, who is alleged to have been subjected to rape or any other sexual offence, is giving evidence?
4335.answer: The court may take appropriate measures to ensure that such woman is not confronted by the accused while at the same time ensuring the right of cross-examination of the accused.

4336.question: Who does the term 'accused' include as per the Code of Criminal Procedure?
4336.answer: The term 'accused' includes a person in relation to whom any proceeding under Chapter VIII has been commenced under the Code.

4337.question: In relation to whom does any proceeding under Chapter VIII commence under the Code of Criminal Procedure?
4337.answer: Any proceeding under Chapter VIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure is commenced in relation to the person termed as 'accused'.

4338.question: What amendment was made to section 273 of the principal Act in Gujarat?
4338.answer: In section 273, after the words 'in the presence of his pleader', the words 'or, as the case may be, through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage when the court on its own motion or on an application so directs in the interests of justice' shall be added.

4339.question: What words were added to section 273 of the principal Act in Gujarat after 'in the presence of his pleader'?
4339.answer: The words 'or, as the case may be, through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage when the court on its own motion or on an application so directs in the interests of justice' were added.

4340.question: What Act introduced the amendment to section 273 of the principal Act in Gujarat?
4340.answer: The amendment was introduced by Gujarat Act 31 of 2017, sec. 2.

4341.question: Which section of the principal Act in Gujarat was amended by Gujarat Act 31 of 2017, sec. 2?
4341.answer: Section 273 of the principal Act was amended by Gujarat Act 31 of 2017, sec. 2.

4342.question: What does section 274 of the Code of Criminal Procedure state?
4342.answer: Section 274 states that in all summons-cases tried before a Magistrate, in all inquiries under sections 145 to 148, and in all proceedings under section 446 otherwise than in the course of a trial, the Magistrate shall, as the examination of each witness proceeds, make a memorandum of the substance of the evidence in the language of the Court.

4343.question: Which section of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires the Magistrate to make a memorandum of the substance of the evidence in the language of the Court as the examination of each witness proceeds in all summons-cases, inquiries under sections 145 to 148, and proceedings under section 446 that are not in the course of a trial?
4343.answer: This is stated in section 274 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

4344.question: What should be done if a magistrate is unable to record the reason of his inability?
4344.answer: A memorandum should be made in writing or from his dictation in open court.

4345.question: What should be the procedure if a magistrate can't record the reason for his inability?
4345.answer: A memorandum should be made in writing or from his dictation in open court.

4346.question: What does the memorandum signed by the Magistrate become a part of?
4346.answer: The memorandum becomes part of the record.

4347.question: What does the record include that is signed by the Magistrate?
4347.answer: The record includes the memorandum signed by the Magistrate.

4348.question: In warrant-cases tried before a Magistrate, how should the evidence of each witness be recorded?
4348.answer: The evidence should be taken down in writing either by the Magistrate himself or by his dictation in open Court or, if he is unable to do so due to a physical or other incapacity, under his direction and superintendence, by an officer of the Court appointed by him.

4349.question: Who should take down the evidence in writing in warrant-cases tried before a Magistrate if the Magistrate is unable to do so due to a physical or other incapacity?
4349.answer: An officer of the Court appointed by the Magistrate should take down the evidence under his direction and superintendence.

4350.question: Can the evidence of a witness be recorded by audio-video electronic means in warrant-cases?
4350.answer: Yes, the evidence of a witness can also be recorded by audio-video electronic means in the presence of the advocate of the person accused of the offence.

4351.question: In the presence of whose advocate can the evidence of a witness be recorded by audio-video electronic means in warrant-cases?
4351.answer: The evidence of a witness can be recorded by audio-video electronic means in the presence of the advocate of the person accused of the offence.

4352.question: What is the Magistrate supposed to do if he causes the evidence to be taken down?
4352.answer: The Magistrate should record a certificate that the evidence could not be taken down by himself for the reasons referred to.

4353.question: What should the Magistrate record if he could not take down the evidence for certain reasons?
4353.answer: The Magistrate should record a certificate that the evidence could not be taken down by himself for the reasons referred to.

4354.question: How is the evidence usually taken down according to the sub-section (1)?
4354.answer: Such evidence shall ordinarily be taken down in the form of a narrative.

4355.question: What is the form in which evidence is typically recorded according to sub-section (1)?
4355.answer: The evidence is usually taken down in the form of a narrative.

4356.question: What can the Magistrate do with the evidence in his discretion?
4356.answer: The Magistrate may, in his discretion take down, or cause to be taken down, any part of such evidence in the form of question and answer.

4357.question: In what form can a Magistrate take down the evidence in his discretion?
4357.answer: The Magistrate may take down the evidence in the form of question and answer.

4358.question: Who signs the evidence that has been taken down?
4358.answer: The evidence so taken down shall be signed by the Magistrate.

4359.question: Who is responsible for signing the evidence that has been taken down?

4360.question: Who takes down the evidence in a trial before a Court of Session?
4360.answer: In all trials before a Court of Session, the evidence of each witness shall, as his examination proceeds, be taken down in writing either by the presiding Judge himself or by his dictation in open Court, or under his direction and superintendence, by an officer of the Court appointed by him in this behalf.

4361.question: How is the evidence of each witness taken down during trials before a Court of Session?
4361.answer: The evidence of each witness is taken down in writing either by the presiding Judge himself or by his dictation in open Court, or under his direction and superintendence, by an officer of the Court appointed by him in this behalf.

4362.question: What can the presiding Judge do with the evidence?
4362.answer: The presiding Judge may, in his discretion, take down, or cause to be taken down, any part of such evidence in the form of question and answer.

4363.question: Who has the discretion to take down, or cause to be taken down, any part of such evidence in the form of question and answer?
4363.answer: The presiding Judge has the discretion to do this.

4364.question: Who signs the evidence taken down in a trial before a Court of Session?
4364.answer: The evidence so taken down shall be signed by the presiding Judge.

4365.question: Who is required to sign the evidence that has been taken down during a trial before a Court of Session?

4366.question: What happens when evidence under section 275 or 276 is completed?
4366.answer: As the evidence of each witness taken under section 275 or section 276 is completed, it shall be read over to him in the presence of the accused, if in attendance, or of his pleader, if he appears by pleader, and shall, if necessary, be corrected.

4367.question: What should be done after the evidence of each witness taken under section 275 or section 276 is completed?
4367.answer: It shall be read over to him in the presence of the accused, if in attendance, or of his pleader, if he appears by pleader, and shall, if necessary, be corrected.

4368.question: What if the witness denies the correctness of any part of the evidence when it is read over to him?
4368.answer: If the witness denies the correctness of any part of the evidence when the same is read over to him, the Magistrate or presiding Judge may, instead of correcting the evidence, make a memorandum thereon of the objection made to it by the witness and shall add such remarks as he thinks necessary.

4369.question: What action can the Magistrate or presiding Judge take if a witness denies the correctness of any part of the evidence when it is read over to him?
4369.answer: The Magistrate or presiding Judge may, instead of correcting the evidence, make a memorandum thereon of the objection made to it by the witness and shall add such remarks as he thinks necessary.

4370.question: What happens if the evidence is in a language different from that in which it has been given?
4370.answer: The text does not provide a specific action for when the record of the evidence is in a language different from that in which it has been given.

4371.question: Does the text provide a specific action for when the record of the evidence is in a language different from that in which it has been given?
4371.answer: No, the text does not provide a specific action for when the record of the evidence is in a language different from that in which it has been given.

4372.question: What happens when under clause (b) evidence is taken down in English and a translation thereof in the language of the Court is not required by any of the parties?
4372.answer: When under clause (b) evidence is taken down in English and a translation thereof in the language of the Court is not required by any of the parties, the Court may dispense with such translation.

4373.question: What may the Court do if under clause (b) evidence is taken down in English and a translation thereof in the language of the Court is not required by any of the parties?
4373.answer: The Court may dispense with such translation.

4374.question: What is the amendment to the principal Act in Gujarat?
4374.answer: In the principal Act, in section 278, after sub-section (3), the following sub-sections shall be added: — '(4) Nothing contained in sub-sections (1) to (3) shall apply when the evidence under section 273 is taken through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage. (5) The evidence taken through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage in electronic from shall be the electronic record within the meaning of clause (t) of section 2 if the Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000)'

4375.question: What is added to section 278 after sub-section (3) in the amendment to the principal Act in Gujarat?
4375.answer: The following sub-sections are added: — '(4) Nothing contained in sub-sections (1) to (3) shall apply when the evidence under section 273 is taken through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage. (5) The evidence taken through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage in electronic from shall be the electronic record within the meaning of clause (t) of section 2 if the Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000)'

4376.question: What happens if the accused does not understand the language of the evidence presented?
4376.answer: Whenever any evidence is given in a language not understood by the accused, and he is present in Court in person, it shall be interpreted to him in open Court in a language understood by him.

4377.question: What should be done if evidence is given in a language not understood by the accused when he is present in Court?
4377.answer: It shall be interpreted to him in open Court in a language understood by him.

4378.question: What is the meaning of evidence taken through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage according to the Gujarat amendment?
4378.answer: The evidence taken through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage in electronic form shall be the electronic record within the meaning of clause (t) of section 2 if the Information Technology Act, 2000.

4379.question: What does the clause (t) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 refer to as per the Gujarat amendment?
4379.answer: The clause (t) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 refers to the evidence taken through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage in electronic form.

4380.question: What happens when evidence is given in a language not understood by the pleader?
4380.answer: It shall be interpreted to such pleader in that language.

4381.question: What should be done when a pleader doesn't understand the language of the given evidence?
4381.answer: It shall be interpreted to such pleader in that language.

4382.question: Who has the discretion to interpret documents put for formal proof?
4382.answer: It is in the discretion of the Court to interpret as much thereof as appears necessary.

4383.question: Who has the discretion to interpret as much of the documents put for formal proof as appears necessary?
4383.answer: It is in the discretion of the Court.

4384.question: What is recorded by a Judge or Magistrate when a witness gives evidence?
4384.answer: The presiding Judge or Magistrate records the evidence of a witness and also such remarks as he thinks material respecting the demeanour of such witness whilst under examination.

4385.question: What does the presiding Judge or Magistrate do when a witness is under examination?
4385.answer: The presiding Judge or Magistrate records the evidence of a witness and also such remarks as he thinks material respecting the demeanour of such witness whilst under examination.

4386.question: What happens when the accused is examined by a Metropolitan Magistrate?
4386.answer: The Magistrate makes a memorandum of the substance of the examination of the accused in the language of the Court and such memorandum is signed by the Magistrate and forms part of the record.

4387.question: Who makes a memorandum of the substance of the examination of the accused and in what language is it made?
4387.answer: The Metropolitan Magistrate makes a memorandum of the substance of the examination of the accused in the language of the Court.

4388.question: What occurs when the accused is examined by a Magistrate other than a Metropolitan Magistrate or by a Court?
4388.answer: The text does not provide information on what occurs when the accused is examined by a Magistrate other than a Metropolitan Magistrate or by a Court.

4389.question: Does the text provide information on what occurs when the accused is examined by a Magistrate other than a Metropolitan Magistrate or by a Court?
4389.answer: No, the text does not provide information on what occurs when the accused is examined by a Magistrate other than a Metropolitan Magistrate or by a Court.

4390.question: Who is responsible for recording the examination during a session?
4390.answer: The presiding Judge or Magistrate himself or if he is unable to do so owing to a physical or other incapacity, an officer of the Court appointed by him.

4391.question: Who would take over the responsibility of recording the examination during a session if the presiding Judge or Magistrate is unable to do so due to a physical or other incapacity?
4391.answer: An officer of the Court appointed by him.

4392.question: In what language should the record be, if practicable?
4392.answer: The record should be in the language in which the accused is examined or, if that is not practicable, in the language of the Court.

4393.question: In which languages should the record be, if the accused's language is not practicable?
4393.answer: The record should be in the language of the Court.

4394.question: What should be done if the accused does not understand the language in which the record is written?
4394.answer: The record shall be interpreted to him in a language which he understands, and he shall be at liberty to explain or add to his answers.

4395.question: What should be done if an accused individual does not comprehend the language in which the record is written?
4395.answer: The record should be translated to a language that the accused understands, and they should have the freedom to clarify or expand on their responses.

4396.question: Who should sign the record after the examination?
4396.answer: The record should be signed by the accused and by the Magistrate or presiding Judge.

4397.question: Who should the accused and the Magistrate or presiding Judge sign for?
4397.answer: The accused and the Magistrate or presiding Judge should sign the record after the examination.

4398.question: What should the presiding Judge or Magistrate certify after the examination?
4398.answer: He should certify under his own hand that the examination was taken in his presence and hearing and that the record contains a full and true account of the statement.

4399.question: What does the certification by the presiding Judge or Magistrate after the examination mean?
4399.answer: The certification by the presiding Judge or Magistrate means that the examination was taken in his presence and hearing and that the record contains a full and true account of the statement.

4400.question: What amendment did Gujarat make to section 281, sub-section (6) in the principal Act?
4400.answer: In the principal Act, in section 281, in sub-section (6), after the words “the examination of an accused person”, the words “either through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage or” shall be inserted.

4401.question: What words were inserted after 'the examination of an accused person' in section 281, sub-section (6) of the principal Act by Gujarat amendment?
4401.answer: The words 'either through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage or' were inserted.

4402.question: What is the obligation of an interpreter in a Criminal Court according to section 282?
4402.answer: When the services of an interpreter are required by any Criminal Court for the interpretation of any evidence or statement, he shall be bound to state the true interpretation of such evidence or statement.

4403.question: What should an interpreter do when their services are required by a Criminal Court for the interpretation of any evidence or statement according to section 282?
4403.answer: When the services of an interpreter are required by any Criminal Court for the interpretation of any evidence or statement, he shall be bound to state the true interpretation of such evidence or statement.

4404.question: What does section 283 state about the record in High Court?
4404.answer: Every High Court may, by general rule, prescribe the manner in which the evidence of witnesses and the examination of the accused shall be taken down in cases coming before it, and such evidence and examination shall be taken down in accordance with such rule.

4405.question: What does the High Court prescribe about the manner in which the evidence of witnesses and the examination of the accused should be taken down in cases coming before it, according to section 283?
4405.answer: Section 283 states that every High Court may, by general rule, prescribe the manner in which the evidence of witnesses and the examination of the accused shall be taken down in cases coming before it, and such evidence and examination shall be taken down in accordance with such rule.

4406.question: When can a court or magistrate dispense with the attendance of a witness?
4406.answer: A court or magistrate can dispense with the attendance of a witness whenever it appears in the course of any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code that the examination of a witness is necessary for the ends of justice, and the attendance of such witness cannot be procured without an amount of delay, expense or inconvenience which, under the circumstances of the case, would be unreasonable.

4407.question: Under what circumstances can the court or magistrate decide that the examination of a witness is not necessary for the ends of justice?
4407.answer: The court or magistrate may decide that the examination of a witness is not necessary for the ends of justice if procuring the attendance of the witness would cause an unreasonable amount of delay, expense, or inconvenience given the circumstances of the case.

4408.question: What can a court or magistrate do if the attendance of a witness cannot be procured without unreasonable delay, expense or inconvenience?
4408.answer: The court or magistrate may issue a commission for the examination of the witness in accordance with the provisions of the chapter.

4409.question: What can a court or magistrate do to examine a witness in accordance with the provisions of the chapter?
4409.answer: If the attendance of a witness cannot be procured without unreasonable delay, expense or inconvenience, the court or magistrate may issue a commission for the examination of the witness.

4410.question: What happens if the examination of the President, Vice-President, a Governor of a state, or Administrator of a Union territory as a witness is necessary for the ends of Justice?
4410.answer: A commission shall be issued for the examination of such a witness.

4411.question: What action is taken if the examination of the President, Vice-President, a Governor of a state, or Administrator of a Union territory is deemed necessary for the ends of Justice?
4411.answer: A commission shall be issued for the examination of such a witness.

4412.question: Who should the commission be directed to if the witness is within the territories to which this Code extends?
4412.answer: The commission should be directed to the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or the Chief Judicial Magistrate, within whose local jurisdiction the witness is to be found.

4413.question: To whom should the commission be directed if the witness is to be found within the local jurisdiction of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or the Chief Judicial Magistrate?
4413.answer: If the witness is within the territories to which this Code extends, the commission should be directed to the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

4414.question: To whom should the commission be directed if the witness is in India, but in a State or an area to which this Code does not extend?
4414.answer: The commission should be directed to such Court or officer as the Central Government may, by notification, specify.

4415.question: Who should the commission be directed to if the witness is in India, but in a State or an area to which this Code does not extend, as per the Central Government's notification?
4415.answer: The commission should be directed to such Court or officer.

4416.question: Where should the commission be issued if the witness is in a country or place outside India and arrangements have been made by the Central Government with the Government of such country or place?
4416.answer: The commission should be issued in such form, directed to such Court or officer.

4417.question: To whom or where should the commission be directed if it is to be issued in a foreign country or place with which the Central Government has made arrangements?
4417.answer: The commission should be directed to such Court or officer.

4418.question: Who is responsible for meeting the expenses of the accused, including the pleader's fees, according to the court?
4418.answer: The prosecution is responsible for meeting the expenses of the accused, including the pleader's fees.

4419.question: Who meets the expenses of the accused, including the pleader's fees, in court?
4419.answer: The prosecution meets the expenses of the accused, including the pleader's fees.

4420.question: Who is responsible for the execution of commissions upon receipt?
4420.answer: The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, or Chief Judicial Magistrate or such Metropolitan or Judicial Magistrate as he may appoint in this behalf

4421.question: Who does the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, or Chief Judicial Magistrate or such Metropolitan or Judicial Magistrate appoint to handle the execution of commissions upon receipt?
4421.answer: He may appoint himself or another Metropolitan or Judicial Magistrate in this behalf.

4422.question: What powers does the individual executing the commission have?
4422.answer: They can take down his evidence in the same manner, and may for this purpose exercise the same powers, as in trials or warrant-cases under this Code.

4423.question: In what manner can the individual executing the commission take down evidence and what powers can they exercise for this purpose?
4423.answer: They can take down his evidence in the same manner, and may for this purpose exercise the same powers, as in trials or warrant-cases under this Code.

4424.question: Who can forward any interrogatories in writing when a commission is issued?
4424.answer: The parties to any proceeding under this Code

4425.question: Under which code can the parties to any proceeding forward any interrogatories in writing when a commission is issued?

4426.question: In which cases is it lawful for the Magistrate, Court or officer to examine the witness upon?
4426.answer: When the commission is directed to them, or when the duty of executing it is delegated to them.

4427.question: When is it lawful for the Magistrate, Court or officer to examine the witness?
4427.answer: When the commission is directed to them, or when the duty of executing it is delegated to them.

4428.question: Who can appear before the magistrate, court or officer?
4428.answer: Any such party may appear before such magistrate, Court or Officer by pleader, or if not in custody, in person.

4429.question: Can a party appear before a magistrate, Court or Officer in person if they are not in custody?
4429.answer: Yes, any such party may appear before such magistrate, Court or Officer in person if they are not in custody.

4430.question: What can the said party do in front of the magistrate, court or officer?
4430.answer: They may examine, cross-examine and re-examine the said witness.

4431.question: Who has the ability to examine, cross-examine, and re-examine a witness in front of a magistrate, court or officer?
4431.answer: The said party can do this.

4432.question: What happens after a commission issued under section 284 has been duly executed?
4432.answer: It shall be returned, together with the deposition of the witness examined thereunder, to the Court or Magistrate issuing the commission.

4433.question: What is the procedure for a commission issued under section 284 after it has been duly executed?
4433.answer: It shall be returned, together with the deposition of the witness examined thereunder, to the Court or Magistrate issuing the commission.

4434.question: What can be done with the returned commission and the deposition?
4434.answer: The commission, the return thereto and the deposition shall be open at all reasonable times to inspection of the parties, and may, subject to all just exceptions, be read in evidence in the case by either party, and shall form part of the record.

4435.question: Can the commission, the return thereto, and the deposition be inspected by the parties, read in evidence by either party, and form part of the record, subject to all just exceptions?
4435.answer: Yes, the commission, the return thereto and the deposition shall be open at all reasonable times to inspection of the parties, and may, subject to all just exceptions, be read in evidence in the case by either party, and shall form part of the record.

4436.question: Under what conditions can a deposition be received in evidence at any subsequent stage of the case before another Court?
4436.answer: If it satisfies the conditions prescribed by section 33 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

4437.question: What section of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 prescribes the conditions under which a deposition can be received in evidence at any subsequent stage of the case before another Court?

4438.question: What happens under section 284?
4438.answer: If a commission is issued under section 284, the inquiry, trial or other proceeding may be adjourned for a specified time reasonably sufficient for the execution and return of the commission.

4439.question: What occurs if a commission is issued and a trial, inquiry or other proceeding is adjourned for a specified time under a particular section?
4439.answer: Under section 284, the inquiry, trial or other proceeding may be adjourned for a specified time reasonably sufficient for the execution and return of the commission.

4440.question: What does section 290 pertain to?
4440.answer: Section 290 pertains to the execution of foreign commissions. It states that the provisions of section 286, 287 and 288 related to the execution of a commission and its return apply to commissions issued by any of the Courts, Judges or Magistrates mentioned in the section.

4441.question: Which section states that the provisions of section 286, 287 and 288 related to the execution of a commission and its return apply to commissions issued by any of the Courts, Judges or Magistrates mentioned in the section?
4441.answer: Section 290 states that the provisions of section 286, 287 and 288 related to the execution of a commission and its return apply to commissions issued by any of the Courts, Judges or Magistrates mentioned in the section.

4442.question: Who are the Courts, Judges and Magistrates referred to in sub-section (1) of section 290?
4442.answer: The Courts, Judges and Magistrates referred to in sub-section (1) of section 290 are: (a) any such Court, Judge or Magistrate exercising jurisdiction within an area in India to which this Code does not extend, as specified by the Central Government; (b) any Court, Judge or Magistrate exercising jurisdiction in any such country or place outside India, as specified by the Central Government, and having authority under the law.

4443.question: Who does the Central Government specify as the Courts, Judges and Magistrates exercising jurisdiction within an area in India to which this Code does not extend, and in any such country or place outside India, with authority under the law?
4443.answer: The Courts, Judges and Magistrates specified by the Central Government are those referred to in sub-section (1) of section 290.

4444.question: What does section 291 state about the deposition of a medical witness?
4444.answer: The deposition of civil surgeon or other medical witness, taken and attested by a Magistrate in the presence of the accused, or taken on commission under this Chapter, may be given in evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code, even if the deponent is not called as a witness.

4445.question: What does the law state about the use of a deposition from a civil surgeon or other medical witness in any inquiry, trial, or other proceedings?
4445.answer: Section 291 states that the deposition of civil surgeon or other medical witness, taken and attested by a Magistrate in the presence of the accused, or taken on commission under this Chapter, may be given in evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code, even if the deponent is not called as a witness.

4446.question: What is the court's discretion regarding the examination of the deposition's deponent?
4446.answer: The Court may, if it thinks fit, and shall, on the application of the prosecution or the accused, summon and examine any such deponent as to the subject-matter of his deposition.

4447.question: Who has the authority to summon and examine a deponent regarding the subject matter of their deposition?
4447.answer: The Court has the authority to summon and examine any such deponent, if it thinks fit or on the application of the prosecution or the accused.

4448.question: What amendment did the Gujarat state make to section 291?
4448.answer: In the principal Act, in section 291, in sub-section (1), after the words 'in the presence of accused', the words 'or, as the case may be through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage' shall be inserted.

4449.question: What words were inserted into sub-section (1) of section 291 of the principal Act by the Gujarat state amendment?
4449.answer: After the words 'in the presence of accused', the words 'or, as the case may be through the medium of Electronic Video Linkage' were inserted.

4450.question: What does section 291A pertain to?
4450.answer: Section 291A pertains to the identification report of a Magistrate.

4451.question: Which section pertains to the identification report of a Magistrate?
4451.answer: Section 291A pertains to the identification report of a Magistrate.

4452.question: Under what conditions can a report of identification under the hand of an Executive Magistrate be used as evidence?
4452.answer: A report of identification under the hand of an Executive Magistrate can be used as evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code, although such Magistrate is not called as a witness.

4453.question: In what circumstances can a report of identification under the hand of an Executive Magistrate be used as evidence, even if the Magistrate is not called as a witness?
4453.answer: A report of identification under the hand of an Executive Magistrate can be used as evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code.

4454.question: What is the exception to using a report containing a statement of any suspect or witness as evidence?
4454.answer: Such statement in the report shall not be used under this sub-section except in accordance with the provisions of section 21, section 32, section 33, section 155 or section 157, as the case may be, of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

4455.question: Under which sections of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 can a statement of any suspect or witness in a report be used as evidence?
4455.answer: A statement in the report can be used as evidence under section 21, section 32, section 33, section 155 or section 157, as per the case.

4456.question: What can the court do regarding the subject-matter of the report?
4456.answer: The Court may, if it thinks fit, and shall, on the application of the prosecution or of the accused, summon and examine such Magistrate as to the subject-matter of the said report.

4457.question: What is the court's procedure if the prosecution or the accused apply regarding the subject-matter of a report?
4457.answer: The Court is obligated to summon and examine such Magistrate as to the subject-matter of the said report.

4458.question: What is the significance of a document purporting to be a report under the hand of any officer of any Mint or of any Note Printing Press or of any Security Printing Press?
4458.answer: The document is considered as evidence.

4459.question: What is the status of a document purporting to be a report under the hand of any officer of any Mint or of any Note Printing Press or of any Security Printing Press?
4459.answer: The document is considered as evidence.

4460.question: Who can the Central Government specify to examine and report on matters in any proceeding under this Code?
4460.answer: The Controller of Stamps and Stationery, any officer of any Forensic Department or Division of Forensic Science Laboratory, any Government Examiner of Questioned Documents or any State Examiner of Questioned Documents

4461.answer: The Central Government can specify them to examine and report on matters in any proceeding under this Code.

4463.question: Is it allowed to use the report of specified officers as evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code?

4471.question: Who can grant permission for officers to share the records on which the report is based?

4472.question: Who is permitted to give evidence derived from any unpublished official records?

4473.question: Who are the entities or officers from the Mint, Note Printing Press, Security Printing Press, Forensic Department, Forensic Science Laboratory, Government Examiner of Questioned Documents Organisation, or the State Examiner of Questioned Documents Organisation permitted to do?
4473.answer: They are permitted to give evidence derived from any unpublished official records.

4474.answer: The nature or particulars of any test applied by him in the course of the examination of the matter or thing

4475.question: What is the nature or particulars of any test applied by the mentioned officers in the course of the examination of the matter or thing?
4475.answer: This is not allowed to be disclosed by the officers.

4476.question: What can be used as evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code?
4476.answer: Any document purporting to be a report under the hand of a Government scientific expert to whom this section applies, upon any matter or thing duly submitted to him for examination or analysis and report in the course of any proceeding under this Code

4477.question: What does a document purporting to be a report under the hand of a Government scientific expert upon any matter or thing duly submitted to him for examination or analysis and report in the course of any proceeding under this Code, serve as in an inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code?
4477.answer: It can be used as evidence.

4478.question: Who can submit a report for examination or analysis in the course of any proceeding under this Code?
4478.answer: A Government scientific expert to whom this section applies

4479.question: To whom does this section apply for submitting a report for examination or analysis in the course of any proceeding under this Code?

4480.answer: Any such expert as to the subject-matter of his report

4481.question: Who is the person that the Court can summon and examine regarding the subject-matter of his report?

4482.question: What can an expert do if he is unable to attend the Court summons personally?
4482.answer: He may depute any responsible officer working with him to attend the Court, if such officer is conversant with the facts of the case and can satisfactorily depose in Court on his behalf

4483.question: Who can attend the Court on behalf of an expert who is unable to attend the summons personally?
4483.answer: Any responsible officer working with him who is conversant with the facts of the case and can satisfactorily depose in Court on his behalf

4487.question: Who is the Chemical Examiner or Assistant Chemical Examiner to Government, the Chief Controller of Explosives, the Director of the Finger Print Bureau, the Director of Haffkeine Institute in Bombay, the Director, Deputy Director or Assistant Director of a Central Forensic Science Laboratory or a State Forensic Science Laboratory, the Serologist to the Government?

4489.question: Who has the authority to specify any other Government scientific expert for a specific purpose?

4490.question: What should be included in a list when any document is filed before any Court?
4490.answer: The particulars of every such document

4491.question: What should be included in a list when filing a document before any Court?
4491.answer: The particulars of every such document

4492.question: Who is called upon to admit or deny the genuineness of each document in court?
4492.answer: The prosecution or the accused, or the pleader for the prosecution or the accused

4493.question: Who may be called upon to admit or deny the genuineness of each document in court situations?
4493.answer: The prosecution or the accused, or the pleader for the prosecution or the accused

4494.question: In what form should the list of documents be?
4494.answer: In such form as be prescribed by the State Government

4495.question: Who prescribes the form in which the list of documents should be?

4496.question: What can be done when the genuineness of any document is not disputed?
4496.answer: Such document may be read in evidence in inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code without proof of the signature of the person to whom it purports to be signed

4497.question: What happens to a document whose genuineness is undisputed in an inquiry, trial, or other proceeding under this Code?
4497.answer: Such document may be read in evidence without proof of the signature of the person to whom it purports to be signed

4498.question: Can the court require the signature on a document to be proved?
4498.answer: Yes, the Court may, in its discretion, require such signature to be proved

4499.question: Who has the discretion to require a signature on a document to be proved?
4499.answer: The Court has the discretion to require such signature to be proved.

4500.question: What can the applicant provide as evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under the Code?
4500.answer: The applicant may give evidence of the facts alleged in the application by affidavit.

4501.question: What method can the applicant use to give evidence of the facts alleged in the application under the Code?
4501.answer: The applicant may provide evidence by affidavit in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding.

4502.question: How can evidence of a formal character be given?
4502.answer: The evidence of a formal character may be given by affidavit.

4503.question: What method is used to give evidence of a formal character?
4503.answer: The evidence of a formal character is given by affidavit.

4504.question: What can the Court do if it finds the facts in an affidavit relevant?
4504.answer: The Court may, if it thinks fit, order that evidence relating to such facts be so given.

4505.question: What action can the Court take if it deems evidence relating to facts from an affidavit to be appropriate?
4505.answer: If the Court finds the facts in an affidavit relevant, it may order that such evidence be given.

4506.question: What can the Court do regarding a person's affidavit?
4506.answer: The Court may, if it thinks fit, and shall, on the application of the prosecution or the accused, summon and examine any such person as to the facts contained in his affidavit.

4507.question: What action may the Court take if the prosecution or the accused applies regarding a person's affidavit?
4507.answer: The Court may summon and examine any such person as to the facts contained in his affidavit.

4508.question: Before whom can affidavits to be used in Court under this Code be sworn or affirmed?
4508.answer: Affidavits can be sworn or affirmed before any Judge or Judicial or Executive Magistrate.

4509.question: Who can affidavits to be used in Court under this Code be sworn or affirmed before?
4509.answer: Any Judge or Judicial or Executive Magistrate.

4510.question: Who can be appointed as a Commissioner of Oaths?
4510.answer: A Commissioner of Oaths can be appointed by a High Court or Court of Session, or any notary appointed under the Notaries Act, 1952.

4511.question: Who can appoint a Commissioner of Oaths?
4511.answer: A Commissioner of Oaths can be appointed by a High Court or Court of Session, or any notary appointed under the Notaries Act, 1952.

4512.question: What should an affidavit contain according to the mentioned code?
4512.answer: Affidavits should be confined to, and state separately, such facts as the deponent is able to prove from his own knowledge and such facts as he has reasonable ground to believe to be true.

4513.question: What facts should be stated in an affidavit according to the deponent's knowledge?
4513.answer: Affidavits should be confined to, and state separately, such facts as the deponent is able to prove from his own knowledge and such facts as he has reasonable ground to believe to be true.

4514.question: What does the deponent need to do if he presents facts based on belief?
4514.answer: In the case of presenting facts based on belief, the deponent shall clearly state the grounds of such belief.

4515.question: What should the deponent do when presenting facts based on belief?
4515.answer: The deponent shall clearly state the grounds of such belief.

4516.question: What can the Court do to any scandalous and irrelevant matter in the affidavit?
4516.answer: The Court may order any scandalous and irrelevant matter in the affidavit to be struck out or amended.

4517.question: What can the Court order for any scandalous and irrelevant matter in the affidavit?
4517.answer: The Court may order any scandalous and irrelevant matter in the affidavit to be struck out or amended.

4518.question: How can a previous conviction or acquittal be proved under this Code?
4518.answer: A previous conviction or acquittal can be proved, in addition to any other mode provided by any law for the time being.

4519.question: Can a previous conviction or acquittal be proved in any other way apart from what is provided by any law for the time being?
4519.answer: Yes, under this Code, a previous conviction or acquittal can be proved.

4520.question: What can be used as evidence in court regarding a conviction or acquittal?
4520.answer: An extract certified under the hand of the officer having the custody of the records of the Court in which such conviction or acquittal was held, a certificate signed by the officer in charge of the Jail in which the punishment or any part thereof was undergone, or the warrant of commitment under which the punishment was suffered

4521.question: What do an extract certified by the officer having the custody of court records, a certificate signed by the jail officer, and the warrant of commitment signify in a court case?
4521.answer: These can be used as evidence in court regarding a conviction or acquittal.

4522.question: What additional evidence is required in such cases?
4522.answer: Evidence as to the identity of the accused person with the person so convicted or acquitted.

4523.question: What type of evidence is needed to confirm the identity of the accused person with the person previously convicted or acquitted in such cases?

4524.question: What does section 299 refer to in the absence of the accused?
4524.answer: If an accused person has absconded, and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, the Court may, in his absence, examine the witnesses produced on behalf of the prosecution, record their depositions and any such deposition may, on the arrest.

4525.question: What happens if an accused person has absconded and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him according to the court?
4525.answer: Section 299 refers to a situation where if an accused person has absconded, and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, the Court may, in his absence, examine the witnesses produced on behalf of the prosecution, record their depositions and any such deposition may, on the arrest.

4526.question: What can the court do if there is no immediate prospect of arresting an absconded accused person?
4526.answer: The court may examine the witnesses produced on behalf of the prosecution, record their depositions and any such deposition may be used on the arrest of the accused person.

4527.question: What actions may the court take regarding witnesses and depositions in the event an absconded accused person cannot be immediately arrested?
4527.answer: The court may examine the witnesses produced on behalf of the prosecution, record their depositions and any such deposition may be used on the arrest of the accused person.

4528.question: What circumstances allow for a deponent's evidence to be used in court?
4528.answer: The deponent's evidence can be used if the deponent is dead or incapable of giving evidence or cannot be found or his presence cannot be procured without an amount of delay, expense or inconvenience which, under the circumstances of the case, would be unreasonable.

4529.question: Under what conditions can the deponent's evidence be used in court if the deponent is dead, incapable of giving evidence, cannot be found, or his presence cannot be procured without an unreasonable amount of delay, expense or inconvenience?
4529.answer: These circumstances allow for a deponent's evidence to be used in court.

4530.question: Who can direct an inquiry if an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment is committed by unknown individuals?
4530.answer: The High Court or the Sessions Judge can direct that any Magistrate of the first class shall hold an inquiry.

4531.question: Who can a High Court or Sessions Judge direct to hold an inquiry if an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment is committed by unknown individuals?
4531.answer: Any Magistrate of the first class

4532.question: Under what conditions can depositions from an inquiry be used against someone subsequently accused of the offence?
4532.answer: The depositions can be used if the deponent is dead or incapable of giving evidence or beyond the limits of India.

4533.question: In what scenarios can the depositions from an inquiry be used against someone accused of the offence?
4533.answer: The depositions can be used if the deponent is dead, incapable of giving evidence, or beyond the limits of India.

4534.question: What does Chapter XXIV discuss?
4534.answer: Chapter XXIV discusses general provisions as to inquiries and trials.

4535.question: Which chapter discusses general provisions as to inquiries and trials?
4535.answer: Chapter XXIV discusses general provisions as to inquiries and trials.

4536.question: What does section 300 state?
4536.answer: Section 300 states that a person once convicted or acquitted is not to be tried for the same offence.

4537.question: Which section states that a person once convicted or acquitted is not to be tried for the same offence?

4538.question: Can a person be tried again for the same offence if they have been convicted or acquitted by a Court of competent jurisdiction?
4538.answer: No, while such conviction or acquittal remains in force, a person cannot be tried again for the same offence.

4539.question: Can a person be tried again for the same offence while such conviction or acquittal remains in force?
4539.answer: No, a person cannot be tried again for the same offence if they have been convicted or acquitted by a Court of competent jurisdiction.

4540.question: Can a person be tried again on the same facts for any other offence?
4540.answer: No, a person cannot be tried again on the same facts for any other offence for which a different charge from the one made against him might have been made.

4541.question: Can a person be tried for a different charge from the one made against him on the same facts for any other offence?
4541.answer: No, a person cannot be tried again on the same facts for any other offence for which a different charge from the one made against him might have been made.

4542.question: Can a person acquitted or convicted of any offence be afterwards tried for any distinct offence?
4542.answer: Yes, with the consent of the State Government, a person acquitted or convicted of any offence may be afterwards tried for any distinct offence.

4543.question: Can a person who has been acquitted or convicted of an offence be tried again for a distinct offence with the consent of the State Government?

4544.question: Can a person be tried for a different offence constituted by any act causing consequences, if they were already convicted of another offence?
4544.answer: Yes, a person convicted of any offence constituted by an act causing consequences, which together with such act constituted a different offence from that of which he was convicted, may be afterwards tried for such last mentioned offence.

4545.question: If a person is convicted of an offence constituted by an act causing consequences, which together with such act constituted a different offence from that of which he was convicted, can they be afterwards tried for such last mentioned offence?
4545.answer: Yes, a person can be tried for a different offence constituted by any act causing consequences, if they were already convicted of another offence.

4546.question: Can a person acquitted or convicted of any offence be subsequently charged with, and tried for, any other offence constituted by the same acts?
4546.answer: Yes, a person acquitted or convicted of any offence can be subsequently charged with, and tried for, any other offence constituted by the same acts if the Court by which he was first tried was not competent to try the offence with which he is subsequently charged.

4547.question: Under what circumstances can a person acquitted or convicted of any offence be subsequently charged with, and tried for, any other offence constituted by the same acts?
4547.answer: A person acquitted or convicted of any offence can be subsequently charged with, and tried for, any other offence constituted by the same acts if the Court by which he was first tried was not competent to try the offence with which he is subsequently charged.

4548.question: Can a person discharged under section 258 be tried again for the same offence?
4548.answer: A person discharged under section 258 shall not be tried again for the same offence except with the consent of the Court by which he was discharged or of any other Court to which the first-mentioned Court is subordinate.

4549.question: Under what conditions can a person discharged under section 258 be tried again for the same offence?
4549.answer: A person discharged under section 258 can be tried again for the same offence only with the consent of the Court by which he was discharged or of any other Court to which the first-mentioned Court is subordinate.

4550.question: Does this section affect the provisions of section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 or of section 188 of this Code?
4550.answer: No, nothing in this section shall affect the provisions of section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 or of section 188 of this Code.

4551.question: Does anything in this section affect the provisions of section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 or of section 188 of this Code?

4552.question: Is the dismissal of a complaint, or the discharge of the accused, an acquittal?
4552.answer: No, the dismissal of a complaint, or the discharge of the accused, is not an acquittal.

4553.question: Is it true that the dismissal of a complaint, or the discharge of the accused, equates to an acquittal?
4553.answer: No, it is not true. The dismissal of a complaint, or the discharge of the accused, does not equate to an acquittal.

4554.question: Can A be charged again with theft as a servant after being aquitted from the same charge?
4554.answer: No, A cannot be charged again with theft as a servant if the acquittal remains in force.

4555.question: If A's acquittal remains in force, can they be charged again with theft as a servant?
4555.answer: No, A cannot be charged again with theft as a servant if the acquittal remains in force.

4556.question: If the person A was convicted of causing grievous hurt to dies, can A be tried again?
4556.answer: Yes, A may be tried again for culpable homicide.

4557.question: If A is tried again for culpable homicide, what previous conviction could A have had?
4557.answer: A could have been previously convicted of causing grievous hurt.

4558.question: Can A be tried again for the murder of B after being convicted of B's culpable homicide?
4558.answer: No, A may not afterwards be tried on the same facts for the murder of B.

4559.question: After being convicted of B's culpable homicide, can A be tried on the same facts for the murder of B?

4560.question: Can A be tried for voluntarily causing grievous hurt to B after being convicted of voluntarily causing hurt to B?
4560.answer: No, A may not be tried for voluntarily causing grievous hurt to B on the same facts, unless the case comes within sub-section (3) of this section.

4561.question: Can A be tried again for voluntarily causing grievous hurt to B on the same facts after being convicted, unless the case comes within sub-section (3) of the section?
4561.answer: No, A cannot be tried again on the same facts for voluntarily causing grievous hurt to B after being convicted.

4562.question: Can A be charged again after being convicted of theft of property from the person of B by a Magistrate of the second class?
4562.answer: The text does not provide a complete answer to this question.

4563.question: Does the text provide a complete answer to whether A can be charged again after being convicted of theft of property from the person of B by a Magistrate of the second class?
4563.answer: No, the text does not provide a complete answer to this question.

4564.question: Who can appear and plead without any written authority in a Court?
4564.answer: The Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor in charge of a case

4565.question: Who is in charge of a case and can appear and plead without any written authority in a court?
4565.answer: The Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor

4566.question: What happens if a private person instructs a pleader to prosecute in a Court?
4566.answer: The Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor in charge of the case shall conduct the prosecution, and the pleader so instructed shall act therein under the directions of the Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor, and may, with the permission of the Court, submit written arguments after the evidence is closed in the case.

4567.question: Who conducts the prosecution when a private person instructs a pleader to prosecute in a Court, and how does the pleader act in this situation?
4567.answer: The Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor in charge of the case conducts the prosecution. The pleader so instructed acts under the directions of the Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor, and may, with the permission of the Court, submit written arguments after the evidence is closed in the case.

4568.question: Can A, B and C be charged again after being convicted by a Magistrate of the first class for robbing D?
4568.answer: A, B and C may afterwards be charged with, and tried for, dacoity on the same facts.

4569.question: Can A, B and C be charged with, and tried for, dacoity on the same facts after being convicted by a Magistrate of the first class for robbing D?
4569.answer: Yes, A, B and C may afterwards be charged again after being convicted.

4570.question: Who can appear and plead without any written authority in a court case under inquiry, trial, or appeal?
4570.answer: The Public Prosecutor in charge of a case

4571.question: Under what circumstances is the Public Prosecutor in charge of a case allowed to appear and plead without any written authority?
4571.answer: In a court case under inquiry, trial, or appeal

4572.question: Can the Assistant Public Prosecutor appear and plead without any written authority in a court case under inquiry or trial?

4573.question: Is it allowed for the Assistant Public Prosecutor to appear and plead without any written authority in a court case under inquiry or trial?

4574.question: Who can a Magistrate permit to conduct prosecution?
4574.answer: Any person other than a police officer below the rank of inspector

4575.question: Who is permitted by a Magistrate to conduct prosecution, other than a police officer below the rank of inspector?

4576.question: Who is not entitled to conduct prosecution without permission?
4576.answer: Any person other than the Advocate-General or Government Advocate or a Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor

4577.question: Who is entitled to conduct prosecution without needing permission?
4577.answer: The Advocate-General, Government Advocate, Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor

4578.question: Can a police officer conduct the prosecution if he has taken part in the investigation into the offence?

4579.question: Is it allowed for a police officer to conduct the prosecution if they have taken part in the investigation into the offence?

4580.question: Who may conduct the prosecution?
4580.answer: Any person conducting the prosecution may do so personally or by a pleader.

4581.question: Who can conduct the prosecution personally or by a pleader?
4581.answer: Any person conducting the prosecution may do so.

4582.question: Who has the right to be defended by a pleader of their choice?
4582.answer: Any person accused of an offence before a Criminal Court, or against whom proceedings are instituted under this Code.

4583.question: Who can select a pleader of their choice when accused of an offence before a Criminal Court, or if proceedings are instituted under this Code?

4584.question: What happens if an accused person in a trial before the Court of Session is not represented by a pleader and does not have sufficient means to engage one?
4584.answer: The Court shall assign a pleader for his defence at the expense of the State.

4585.question: Who pays for the defense of an accused person in a trial before the Court of Session if they are not represented by a pleader and do not have sufficient means to engage one?
4585.answer: The expense for the assigned pleader for the accused person's defense is covered by the State.

4586.question: Who can make rules for selecting pleaders for defence, facilities to be allowed to such pleaders by the Courts, and the fees payable to such pleaders?
4586.answer: The High Court may, with the previous approval of the State Government, make these rules.

4587.question: Who can make rules for selecting pleaders for defence, facilities to be allowed to such pleaders by the Courts, and the fees payable to such pleaders with the previous approval of the State Government?
4587.answer: The High Court may make these rules.

4588.question: Who can the State Government direct to apply the provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2)?
4588.answer: Any class of trials before other Courts in the State

4589.question: Before which courts in the State can the provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2) be applied as directed by the State Government?
4589.answer: Any class of trials before other Courts in the State

4590.question: What does the term 'corporation' refer to according to section 305?
4590.answer: An incorporated company or other body corporate, including a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860

4591.question: Which section refers to an incorporated company or other body corporate, including a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 as 'corporation'?

4592.question: What can a corporation do if it is the accused person or one of the accused persons in an inquiry or trial?
4592.answer: It may appoint a representative for the purpose of the inquiry or trial

4593.question: Who can a corporation appoint if it is accused in an inquiry or trial?
4593.answer: It may appoint a representative for the purpose of the inquiry or trial

4594.question: Does the appointment of the representative need to be under the seal of the corporation?

4595.question: Is it necessary for the appointment of the representative to be under the seal of the corporation?

4596.question: What happens when a representative of a corporation appears?
4596.answer: Any requirement of this Code that anything shall be done in the presence of the accused or shall be read

4597.question: What is required by the Code when something needs to be done in the presence of the accused or read?
4597.answer: A representative of a corporation appears

4598.question: What happens if the representative of a corporation does not appear?
4598.answer: Any such requirement as is referred to in sub-section (3) shall not apply.

4599.question: What happens when the requirement referred to in sub-section (3) does not apply?
4599.answer: This usually happens if the representative of a corporation does not appear.

4600.question: What is construed as a requirement for the representative?
4600.answer: That thing shall be done in the presence of the representative or read or stated or explained to the representative, and any requirement that the accused shall be examined shall be construed as a requirement that the representative shall be examined.

4601.question: What does it mean when it is required that the accused shall be examined in the presence of the representative?
4601.answer: It means that the same requirement applies to the representative, meaning the representative should also be examined. This also implies that everything should be done in the presence of the representative or read, stated, or explained to them.

4602.question: What is the effect of a written statement signed by the managing director or any person managing the affairs of the corporation?
4602.answer: The Court shall, unless the contrary is proved, presume that such person has been so appointed as the representative of the corporation for the purposes of this section.

4603.question: What is presumed by the Court when a person managing the affairs of the corporation signs a written statement, unless proven otherwise?
4603.answer: The Court shall presume that such person has been appointed as the representative of the corporation for the purposes of this section.

4604.question: What happens when a statement in writing is filed purporting to be signed by the managing director of the corporation?
4604.answer: The Court shall, unless the contrary is proved, presume that the person named in the statement has been appointed as the representative of the corporation for the purposes of this section.

4605.question: What presumption does the court make unless the contrary is proved when a statement is filed purporting to be signed by the managing director of a corporation?
4605.answer: The Court shall presume that the person named in the statement has been appointed as the representative of the corporation for the purposes of this section.

4606.question: Who determines whether a person appearing as the representative of a corporation in an inquiry or trial before a Court is or is not such representative?
4606.answer: The question is determined by the Court.

4607.question: Who determines if a person is a valid representative of a corporation in an inquiry or trial?

4608.question: What does section 306 talk about?
4608.answer: Section 306 discusses the tender of pardon to an accomplice with a view to obtaining evidence of any person supposed to have been directly or indirectly involved in an offence.

4609.question: Which section discusses the tender of pardon to an accomplice with a view to obtaining evidence of any person supposed to have been directly or indirectly involved in an offence?

4610.question: Who can tender a pardon according to section 306?
4610.answer: The Chief Judicial Magistrate, a Metropolitan Magistrate at any stage of the investigation or inquiry into, or the trial of, the offence, and the Magistrate of the first class inquiring into or trying the offence, can tender a pardon.

4611.question: Who, at any stage of the investigation or inquiry into, or the trial of, the offence, can tender a pardon according to section 306?
4611.answer: The Chief Judicial Magistrate, a Metropolitan Magistrate, and the Magistrate of the first class inquiring into or trying the offence, can tender a pardon.

4612.question: What condition is set for the person being pardoned according to section 306?
4612.answer: The person must make a full and true disclosure of the whole of the circumstances within his knowledge relative to the offence and to every other person concerned, whether as principal or abettor, in the commission of the offence.

4613.question: What does section 306 require from the person seeking pardon in relation to the disclosure of circumstances and involvement of others in the offence?
4613.answer: Section 306 requires the person seeking pardon to make a full and true disclosure of the whole of the circumstances within his knowledge relative to the offence and to every other person concerned, whether as principal or abettor, in the commission of the offence.

4928.question: What can the Magistrate do to whom the case is submitted?
4928.answer: The Magistrate to whom the case is submitted may, if so empowered, either try the case himself, or refer it to any Magistrate subordinate to him having jurisdiction, or commit the accused for trial.

4929.question: Who can try the case, refer it to a subordinate with jurisdiction, or commit the accused for trial if empowered to do so?
4929.answer: The Magistrate to whom the case is submitted can do this.

4930.answer: He shall stay the proceedings and submit the case, with a brief report explaining its nature, to the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

4931.question: What should a Magistrate do if he believes a case should be tried by the Chief Judicial Magistrate?
4931.answer: He shall stay the proceedings and submit the case, with a brief report explaining its nature, to the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

4932.answer: He should stay the proceedings and submit the case, with a brief report explaining its nature, to the Chief Judicial Magistrate or to such other Magistrate, having jurisdiction, as the Chief Judicial Magistrate directs.

4933.question: What should a Magistrate do if he believes a case should be passed on to another Magistrate in the district for trial?
4933.answer: He should stay the proceedings and submit the case, with a brief report explaining its nature, to the Chief Judicial Magistrate or to such other Magistrate, having jurisdiction, as the Chief Judicial Magistrate directs.

4937.question: What does a Magistrate do when a case is determined to be one that needs to be tried by the Court of Session, and what provisions apply to the commitment made?

4938.question: Under what circumstances can a person be tried for offences against coinage, stamp-law or property?
4938.answer: A person can be tried for offences against coinage, stamp-law or property if they have been previously convicted of an offence punishable under Chapter XII or Chapter XVII of the Indian Penal Code with imprisonment for a term of three years or upwards, and are again accused of any offence punishable under either of those Chapters with imprisonment for a term of three years or upwards.

4939.answer: A person in such circumstances can be tried for offences against coinage, stamp-law or property.

4942.answer: The trial is sent to the Chief Judicial Magistrate or committed to the Court of Session.

4943.answer: It indicates that the Magistrate believes he cannot himself pass an adequate sentence.

4944.answer: Any other person accused jointly in the same inquiry or trial is similarly sent or committed, unless the Magistrate discharges such other person.

4950.question: What can the Chief Judicial Magistrate do upon receiving the proceedings?
4950.answer: The Chief Judicial Magistrate can examine the parties and recall and examine any witness who has already given evidence in the case. 4951.question: What are the responsibilities and powers of the Chief Judicial Magistrate after receiving case proceedings?
4951.answer: The Chief Judicial Magistrate can examine the parties and recall and examine any witness who has already given evidence in the case. 4952.question: What happens if a Magistrate considers it necessary to proceed under sub-section (1) when multiple accused are being tried together?
4952.answer: If the Magistrate considers it necessary to proceed under sub-section (1) when multiple accused are being tried together, he shall forward all the accused, who are in his opinion guilty, to the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

4953.answer: The Magistrate shall forward all the accused, who are in his opinion guilty, to the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

4956.answer: The succeeding judge may act on the evidence so recorded by his predecessor, or partly recorded by his predecessor and partly recorded by himself.

4957.answer: Yes, the succeeding judge may act on the evidence so recorded by his predecessor, or partly recorded by his predecessor and partly recorded by himself.

4958.question: What can the succeeding judge do if he believes that further examination of a witness is necessary?
4958.answer: He may re-summon any such witness, and after such further examination, cross-examination and re-examination, as he may permit, the witness shall be discharged.

4959.question: What happens if a succeeding judge deems further examination of a witness necessary?
4959.answer: The succeeding judge may re-summon the witness, and allow further examination, cross-examination, and re-examination before discharging the witness.

4970.question: What is the provision regarding the conduct of trials under sections 376AB, 376B, 376C, 376D, 376DA, 376DB, and 376E of the Indian Penal Code?
4970.answer: The trials shall be conducted in camera. However, the presiding Judge may, if he thinks fit, or on an application made by either of the parties, allow any particular person to have access to, or be or remain in, the room or building used by the Court.

4971.question: How are trials conducted under sections 376AB, 376B, 376C, 376D, 376DA, 376DB, and 376E of the Indian Penal Code and who can have access to the court room?

4973.answer: The in camera trial shall be conducted as far as practicable by a woman Judge or Magistrate.

4974.answer: It shall not be lawful for any person to print or publish any matter in relation to any such proceedings except with the previous permission of the Court.

4996.question: What should a Magistrate do if they believe the person against whom the inquiry is being held is of unsound mind?
4996.answer: The Magistrate should inquire into the fact of such unsoundness of mind, and cause such person to be examined by the civil surgeon of the district or such other medical officer as the State Government may direct. Thereupon, the Magistrate shall examine such surgeon or other officer as a witness, and reduce the examination to writing.

4997.question: What steps should a Magistrate take if they think a person being inquired into is mentally unstable?
4997.answer: If a Magistrate believes the person in question is mentally unstable, they should first inquire into the person's mental health. They should then arrange for the person to be examined by the district's civil surgeon or a medical officer as directed by the State Government. After the examination, the Magistrate should interview the surgeon or medical officer and record their findings in writing.

4998.question: What happens if the civil surgeon finds the accused to be of unsound mind?

5015.question: What should the Magistrate do under section 330 if no prima facie case is made against the accused?

5020.question: What is the procedure if a person of unsound mind is tried before a court?
5020.answer: If at the trial of any person before a Magistrate or Court of Session, it appears that such person is of unsound mind and consequently incapable of making his defence, the Magistrate or Court shall, in the first instance, try the fact of such unsoundness and incapacity. If the Magistrate or Court, after considering medical and other evidence, is satisfied of the fact, he or it shall record a finding to that effect and postpone further proceedings in the case.

5021.question: What happens when a person appearing to be of unsound mind is tried before a Magistrate or Court of Session?
5021.answer: If at the trial of any person before a Magistrate or Court of Session, it appears that such person is of unsound mind and consequently incapable of making his defence, the Magistrate or Court shall, in the first instance, try the fact of such unsoundness and incapacity. If the Magistrate or Court, after considering medical and other evidence, is satisfied of the fact, he or it shall record a finding to that effect and postpone further proceedings in the case.

5022.answer: If during trial, the Magistrate or Court of Sessions finds the accused to be of unsound mind, he or it shall refer such person to a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist for care and treatment.

5036.answer: If no prima facie case is made out against the accused, the Magistrate or Court shall discharge the accused and deal with him in the manner provided under section 330.

5039.question: What should be done if a prima facie case is established against an accused found to be of unsound mind, according to the discretion of a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist?
5039.answer: The Magistrate or Court shall postpone the trial for such period as is required for the treatment of the accused, as per the opinion of the psychiatrist or clinical psychologist.

5040.question: What should the Magistrate or Court do if a prima facie case is made out against the accused and he is incapable of entering defence due to mental retardation?
5040.answer: If a prima facie case is made out against the accused and he is incapable of entering defence by reason of mental retardation, the Magistrate or Court shall not hold the trial and order the accused to be dealt with in accordance with section 330.

5041.question: What should the Magistrate or Court do if a prima facie case is made out against an accused who is incapable of defence due to mental retardation, according to section 330?
